Sheet0.Site: Kemoo 5 Reservoir, Oahu, HI
Helemano 6 Reservoir, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Helemano 6 Reservoir is located just off of Kamehameha Highway roughly halfway between Wahiawa and Haleiwa and is immediately downstream from Helemano 16 Reservoir (HMNH1). 

Water from this reservoir feeds into Poamoho Stream which enters the ocean between Haleiwa and Waialua. 

DLNR has not provided an alert threshold for this site and we do not have any notification requirements for high water levels.

Sheet0.Site: Upper Helemano Reservoir near Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Opaeula Str nr Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Opaeula Stream is one of Oahu's larger watersheds and also provides one of the higher risks to life and property since it flows through Haleiwa town on the North Shore. 

A flash flood on April 19, 1974 damaged or destroyed 75 homes in Haleiwa and killed 3 people when their home was swept into the swollen stream. 

The December 11, 2008 flash flood damaged 20 homes but no serious injuries or deaths. Peak stage was 14.5 ft in this event. 

The installation of the Opaeula Stream at Haleiwa (OPSH1) gage on the Joseph Leong Highway Bridge for a short period of time provided data on the travel time from OPAH1 to OPSH1. 

Based on data from the January 27, 2013 heavy rain event, it appears that the flood wave takes about 2 hours to travel between the two sites. Thus, a warning based on an alarm at OPAH1 can provide useful lead time to residents in Haleiwa. 

An alarm threshold of 12.2 feet is based on the March 9, 2012 event where water levels reached properties in Haleiwa but did not cause damage.

Sheet0.Site: Kamananui Str at Maunawai, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Kamananui Stream lies within what is more commonly referred to as Waimea Valley along the North Shore of Oahu. The valley includes a park and botanical garden managed by the Office of Hawaiian Affairs. Visitors swim in the stream at Waimea Falls, and also kayak along the lower reach near the park entrance. 

Flood waters have inundated and damaged park structures. There is also a significant landslide risk within the park itself and along Kamehameha Highway near Waimea Bay. Park attractions upstream from the gage may also be affected.


The alarm threshold is set at 10.6 feet based on USGS survey information which indicates that a road on the left bank of the stream near the gage becomes inundated.

Sheet0.Site: Kamananui Str at Pupukea Mil Rd, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes: Threshold not yet established. The rating curve is being developed by the USGS for this location.

Sheet0.Site: Kaluanui Stream nr Punaluu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This stream gage is located in Sacred Falls State Park, though the park remains closed to the public indefinitely following the May 10, 1999 rockslide that killed 6 people. The stream is very flashy and poses a high risk to hikers who trespass into the park but generally does not directly cause inundation problems except for very high flow events. The alarm level of 11 feet is close to the 10-year return period. 

Recent events with flood peaks above 11 feet at the Kaluanui Stream gage have also involved damaging flash floods in nearby stream basins such as Kaipapau Stream, Maakua Gulch, and Waipilopilo Gulch.

Sheet0.Site: Punaluu Str abv Punaluu Ditch Intake, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Punaluu Stream is on the windward side of the Koolau Range of Oahu and drains one of the wettest areas of the island. 

Flooding along the lower reaches of Punaluu Stream has occurred in recent history and Kamehameha Highway is also at risk of closing if water overtops the bridge. High tides and sand berms can also hinder the outflow to the ocean, causing a backwater effect that can compound flooding problems. 

High levels of flow in Punaluu Stream may also be an indirect indicator of flooding problems elsewhere in Punaluu town and in adjacent Hauula. 

The alarm threshold was raised from 7 ft to 10 ft due to a change in the rating curve.

Sheet0.Site: Kahana Str at alt 30 ft nr Kahana, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Kahana Stream lies within a broad, deeply cut valley in the mid-section of the Koolau Range. 

Very high flows can inundate farms and possibly some residences and structure in the lower reaches of the stream. It is not known exactly what stream height begins to inundate properties but it is believed to be over 12 feet stage. 

This alarm stage value can serve as an indirect indicator of flash flooding along the windward coast of Oahu from Kaaawa to Punaluu.

Significant stream channel changes following the March 9, 2021 flash flood resulted in a large shift of the rating curve used by the USGS. The updated alarm stage is 10.0 ft (formerly at 6.0 ft).  The record height of 14.2 feet is a revised peak stage after the rating curve adjustment.

Sheet0.Site: Waikane Str at alt 75 ft at Waikane, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Waikane Stream frequently causes the closing of Kamehameha Highway due to poor outlet conditions and the close proximity of the highway to the ocean. Inundation of the highway can cover a span of greater than 100 yards with some areas more than two feet deep. Closures can last several hours for each event. 

In April 29, 2023, a flash flood with a peak stage of 7.21 ft (761 cfs) closed both lanes of Kamehameha Highway. This followed two events about a week prior with peaks of 6.36 ft and 6.55 ft that did not produce water on the highway. As a result of these events, the alarm threshold was raised to 7.0 feet. The earlier alarm was at 5.0 feet.
Sheet0.EOC Procedures: At 7ft ask HPD to close the road

Sheet0.Site: Waiahole Stream above Kamehameha Hwy, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This stream is located on the windward side of Oahu north of Kaneohe and normally remains within its banks despite the high amounts of rain that can fall in the headwaters of Waiahole Valley. When Waiahole Stream overflows, it can close Kamehameha Highway at Waiahole Valley Road adjacent to the locally well-known poi factory. 

The record-breaking flash flood on June 4, 2011 caused significant damage to agriculture operations in the area and destroyed the USGS stream gage. The period of record is relatively short so return period statistics are unrepresentative. 

The alarm level of 12 ft is based on USGS survey data and indicates an overflow of the stream along the left bank near the gage. 

At 14 ft, the stream is expected to overflow the bridge at Kamehameha Hwy.
Sheet0.EOC Procedures:
At 12ft, begin having HPD monitor for impacts to Kam Hwy.

At 14ft, request HPD close Kam Hwy as the stream is expected to overflow the bridget at Kam Hwy at this level.

Sheet0.Site: Waihee Str nr Kahaluu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This drainage is located near Kahaluu on the windward side of Oahu. 

Flooding is known to occur on properties along Waihee Stream upslope from Ahilama Road but it is not known precisely at what stream level the inundation begins.

In addition to a damaging level of flooding along the banks of Waihee Stream, flooding may also occur along nearby streams and drainages such as Kaalaea Stream to the northwest.

The alarm level has been raised from 6 feet to 7.5 feet (10-year return period) as the 6 ft threshold appeared to be too low based on verification data.

Sheet0.Site: Kahaluu Str nr Ahuimanu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Kahaluu Stream drains the windward slopes of the Koolau Range on Oahu. The stream flows through the Ahuimanu community near Kaneohe. 

Although much of this stream is channelized and concrete lined, there is still a risk of overflow that can inundate properties near Kahekili Highway, especially if debris jams block the flow at the bridges. 

Significant flow in Kahaluu Stream can also be indicative of damaging runoff anywhere from the Valley of the Temples to Waihee Valley. 

The alarm level is set at 6 feet, which is close to the 10-year return period.

Sheet0.Site: Heeia Stream at Haiku Plantations Dr., Oahu, HI
Heeia Stream at Haiku Valley nr Kaneohe, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This stream is located on the windward side of Oahu near Kaneohe and is in the same valley as the H-3 Freeway. 

Although this gage has a long period of record, most of the peak flows occurred from 1940 to 1970 despite some very heavy rain events in more recent years. Some changes in channel conditions upstream from the gage may have resulted in lower flow. 

Very high flow levels may cause flooding problems on Kamehameha Highway near Heeia Pond but it is not known at this time what level of flow it takes to cause this issue. 

The alarm of 5 feet is near the 10-year return period range and is an indirect indicator of possible flooding problems in the Haiku Valley and Kaneohe areas of windward Oahu.

Sheet0.Site: Kaneohe Str blw Kamehameha Hwy, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This is a relatively new stream gage with a short period of record. Kapunahala Stream and Kamooalii Stream are its primary tributaries that drain the Haiku and Hoomaluhia areas, respectively. 

Property damage from flooding has occurred along Kapunahala Stream at Anoi Road. Unfortunately, this occurred in 2004 prior to the Kaneohe Stream gage installation so it is unknown what the level of flow was for the event. 

An alarm has been set for 24 feet, close to peak flow from the 2/18/2018 heavy rain event that produced flooding across portions of windward Oahu.

Sheet0.Site: Kawa Str at Kaneohe, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Kawa Stream drains the southern portion of Kaneohe in the area near the Hawaii State Veteran's Cemetery and Mokulele Drive. 

An alarm level has been set at 9.5 feet, which is between the 5- and 10-year return periods. This is close to the peak levels reached by the June 4, 2011 and February 18, 2018 heavy rain events that produced flooding across portions of windward Oahu.

Sheet0.Site: Kawainui Marsh nr levee sta 15+00, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Kawainui Marsh is located just southwest of Kailua on Oahu. The water level gage is positioned on the marsh levee and was installed as part of the Kawainui Marsh Flood Warning System. The levee actually has two levels. The first level is earthen and tops out at the 10 ft stage level on the gage. A second level consisting of a concrete structure on top of the earthen levee is at the 15 ft stage level. Should the marsh reach the 15 ft stage, flooding of the Coconut Grove subdivision will likely occur. 

Contact the SSH if a Kawainui Marsh alert or alarm is received. If the SSH is not available, contact the Oahu Warning Point and have them notify the City & County of Honolulu Department of Emergency Management that the Kawainui Marsh has exceeded the 7 or 10 ft threshold.
Sheet0.EOC Procedures:
At 7ft - request HPD to begin monitoring

At 12ft and rising - issue IPAWS alert to prepare to evacuate

At 13.5 ft and rising - initiate IPAWS alert and warning and evacuation of Coconut Grove subdivision.

Sheet0.Site: Makawao Str nr Kailua, Oahu, HI
Waimanalo Str at Waimanalo, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes: This stream is located along the windward side of the Koolau Range of Oahu south of Kailua. The stream drains through the town of Waimanalo and Bellows Air Force Station. Large flood events, such as during 12/31/1987 and 4/13/2018 can cause significant damage within Waimanalo Valley. The alarm threshold of 12 feet is set just below the record peak stage of 13.13 feet from the 4/13/2018 event.

Sheet0.Site: Manoa-Palolo Drainage Canal at Moiliili, Oahu, HI
Pukele Stream near Honolulu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Pukele Stream drains the west side of Palolo Valley and merges with Waiomao Stream to form Palolo Stream. 

There are no known direct flood threats from Pukele Stream but at the 5 ft alarm level, there may be significant runoff problems elsewhere in Palolo Valley. This alarm is also within the 2- to 5-year return period range. 

Additionally, there is a potential landslide risk along the east side of the valley which has proven to be unstable in the past.

Sheet0.Site: Manoa Stream at Woodlawn Drive, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This is a gage installed in 2011 near the area of a significant overflow of Manoa Stream during the October 31, 2004 flash flood. Insufficient stream channel capacity, worsened by severe debris jamming at the Woodlawn St. bridge, caused large amounts of water to exit the channel and flow through the University of Hawaii's Manoa Campus. Most of the $100 million in damage attributed to the flood occurred at the UH campus. 

Other areas at risk along Manoa Stream include the Lowry St. area and the reach from Pakanu St. to the Manoa District Park. 

Based on the October 2004 event, significant overflows at the Woodlawn bridge also threaten Manoa Valley from Noelani School downslope to the UH campus. The flash flood event during the early morning of December 13, 2011 provided good benchmarks for impacts. The peak of the event (12.86 feet) resulted in the stream just reaching the top of the Woodlawn St. bridge with some debris pushed onto the sidewalk and road. Flood waters also inundated a nearby property at about the 10.5 ft stage with fast-flowing water and mud moving through the garage. 

For now, the alarm level will be kept at 8 feet, even though damage levels occur at higher stages. One reason is that the gage is very close to the home in the floodway so waiting for the impact stage (10.5 feet) does not provide any lead time. Another key reason is that Manoa Stream can rise very quickly, in some cases as much as 6 feet within the 15-minute time steps of the data logger.

Sheet0.Site: Waiakeakua Str at Honolulu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Waiakeakua Stream is the main eastern tributary of Manoa Stream on Oahu. 

Manoa Stream has a history of producing damaging floods, the most notable recent event being the October 30, 2004 "Manoa Flood" which caused approximately $100 million in damages, mostly on the University of Hawaii campus. 

During the "Manoa Flood" event, the Waiakeakua Stream stage peaked at 4.27 feet, which was approximately the 10-year return period. While this appears to be low considering the magnitude of the flood, the data analysis shows that the heaviest rainfall during this event occurred over the western half of the basin so the lower stream flow at Waiakeakua Stream appears to be reasonable. 

The alarm threshold has been set at 4.0 feet and is within the 2- to 5-year return period range. Manoa Stream can overflow at Woodlawn Drive and at Lowrey Street.

Sheet0.Site: Waihi Stream at Honolulu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Waihi Stream drains the western headwaters of Manoa Valley on Oahu and is one of two primary tributaries to Manoa Stream. The eastern headwaters flow into Waiakeakua Stream, which is also gaged by the USGS (NWS ID: WKGH1). The two gages are separated by only about 100 yards with both streams merging about 100 yards downslope to form Manoa Stream. 

The most notable recent Manoa Stream flood event was on October 30, 2004. This event caused about $100 million in damages, mostly on the University of Hawaii campus. Spikes in flow in Waihi Stream occur only 15 minutes after heavy rainfall is recorded at the Manoa Lyon Arboretum gage (MNLH1), then reaches the Manoa Stream Woodlawn Dr gage 15 minutes later.

The 6.5 ft alarm threshold roughly equates to the 2- to 5-year return period. A stage value of 7.2 ft at Waihi Stream occurred during the December 13, 2011 event which produced property damage at Woodlawn Dr.

Sheet0.Site: Makiki Stream at King St. bridge, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Makiki Stream flows through the heart of Honolulu and has been the cause of significant urban flooding, especially in the Fern St. area of Makiki near Kapiolani Blvd. and Kalakaua Ave.

The period of record for this gage is short, but one of the large recorded flows on October 30, 2004 did cause flooding in Makiki. Another significant flood event in Makiki Stream occurred on March 31, 2006 during the so-called "40 days of rain" and inundated a fairly large area with up to a couple of feet of water. Unfortunately, the gage was removed from service during this time and only returned to service in 2011 so peak flow data are not available for this event.

Sheet0.Site: Kalihi Str nr Honolulu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This stream drains the Koolau Range toward the southwest into Honolulu near the Nimitz industrial area. More than half of its lower reach is surrounded by urbanized land use so the threat of high impact flooding from this waterway is significant, especially near Dillingham Blvd. 

In upper Kalihi Valley, it appears most structures are high enough or far enough away from the stream to prevent being directly impacted by flooding. However, property damage in the valley has occurred from tributary and drainage system flooding which would be indirectly reflected by high water levels in Kalihi Stream. 

The alarm threshold has been set at 10 feet, which is around the 5-year return period. Flooding from the overflow of Kalihi Stream at the Dillingham Blvd bridge and upstream in Kalihi during Tropical Storm Darby in September 2016 caused property damage. 

The peak flow during this event was 2,710 cfs at a stage value of 10.19 feet.

Sheet0.Site: Moanalua Stream nr Kaneohe, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes: Moanalua Stream drains the central Koolau Range into Keehi Lagoon near the Mapunapuna area of Honolulu. Large floods, such as the event on 12/7/2003, can cause significant damage in the Mapunapuna industrial area, Fort Shafter, the Moanalua Gardens park, and on properties along the stream channel in Moanalua Valley. This stream gage has a short period of record due to a large gap in data collection from the mid-1970s to 2013 when the site was restored. The alarm threshold of 9.0 feet is set just below the level reached on 7/24/2016 during the passage of Tropical Storm Darby. Flow at this level is close to the 10-year return period.

Sheet0.Site: South Halawa Stream nr H-3 Freeway, Oahu, HI
N. Halawa Str nr Quar. Stn. at Halawa, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Halawa Stream drains the east-central portion of the Koolau Range into the East Loch of Pearl Harbor. The lower reaches of Halawa Stream are well channelized as a result of previous flooding and there is minimal risk of direct inundation problems. However, high stream levels reported by the gage can be an indirect indicator of flooding elsewhere in Halawa Valley and in neighboring Moanalua Valley and Aiea. 

This gage has a short period of record and reliable return period statistics are not available. For now, the alarm threshold has been set at 10 feet and will be adjusted as needed in the future.

Sheet0.Site: N. Halawa Str nr Honolulu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This gage is upstream from another USGS gage on North Halawa Stream near the Quarantine Station. 

North Halawa Stream drains the east-central portion of the Koolau Range into the East Loch of Pearl Harbor. The lower reaches of North Halawa Stream are well channelized due to previous flooding and there is a minimal risk of inundation problems. 

High stream levels reported by this gage can be an indirect indicator of flooding elsewhere in Halawa Valley, and in adjacent Moanalua Valley to the east and Aiea to the west. 

The current alarm is set at 12.5 feet, which is close to the 10-year return period. The record peak here occurred during the passage of Tropical Storm Darby in July 2016.

Sheet0.Site: Waikele Str at Waipahu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Waikele Stream drains the windward-facing slopes of the Waianae Range to the southwest of Schofield Barracks and Wheeler Airfield. A confluence of Waikele Stream and Kipapa Stream occurs just upslope of the H-1 Freeway near Waipahu. Waikele Stream then flows into West Loch of Pearl Harbor through Waipahu. 

Direct inundation problems do not usually occur along Waikele Stream, though the record-breaking December 11, 2008 flood caused property damage in Waipahu as water overflowed the drainage channel. 

Since the Waikele Stream gage is located below the confluence with Kipapa Stream, the volume of water recorded at this site can be quite large. The alarm threshold for this site has been set at 12.0 feet, which is roughly the 10-year return period.

Sheet0.Site: Waikele Str at Wheeler Field, Oahu, HI
Honouliuli Str at H-1 Freeway nr Waipahu, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Honouliuli Stream starts in the southeastern slopes of the Waianae Range on Oahu and flows into the West Loch portion of Pearl Harbor. 

The lower reach of the stream flows through the Honouliuli community between Fort Weaver Road and Old Fort Weaver Road. Significant property damage has occurred, most recently in December 11, 2008 and January 12, 2011. 

Large flows can overtop the bridge near the intersection of Weaver Road and Old Fort Weaver Road. 

The Honouliuli Stream gage near H-1 is a new site with a very short period of record. As a result, there is currently no alarm threshold set for this gage. 

Another gage, Honouliuli Stream (SID: HOUH1), is located farther upslope. Although it only has a slightly longer period of record, it has captured some peak flows and can provide more usable lead time since it is farther from populated areas.

Sheet0.Site: Kaupuni Str at alt 374 ft nr Waianae, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Kaupuni Stream is located within Waianae Valley. The gage is located on the portion of the stream just above the low water crossing over Haleahi Road. 

The valley is sparsely populated above the low water crossing and flooding at this location will not impact many people other than a few local residents and farmers. The stream becomes channelized along the lower reaches and is not a known recent flood threat in the more populated areas of the valley. However, high flows at the gage would be indicative of other flooding issues within Waianae Valley, such as along Waianae Valley Road. 

The alarm level of 5 ft is based on a small sample size, but is higher than the 4.62 ft on February 20, 2023 where heavy rainfall occurred in Waianae Valley but did not produce notable flooding impacts.

Sheet0.Site: Makaha Str nr Makaha, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
Makaha Stream drains the west-facing slopes of the Waianae Range on Oahu. 

The main risk for direct inundation appears to be near the coast at Farrington Highway. Otherwise, high water levels at the Makaha Stream gage would be indirectly indicative of flood problems across Makaha Valley. 

Most of the properties are near the coast, though the Makaha Valley Towers condominium complex near the north wall of the valley has been damaged by flooding. 

The 5 ft alarm threshold set for this site is close to the 5- to 10-year return period for flow.

Sheet0.Site: Kaukonahua Str at Waialua, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This gage started providing real-time data on September 14, 2012 and samples Kaukonahua Stream near Otake Camp in Waialua. 

The gage was installed at the site of a crest stage gage so the historical peak flow data values were used to determine an alarm threshold. 

One issue with this gage is that it is downstream from the flood prone area so it will not provide useful flash flood warning lead times. It will be useful to help determine flood wave travel times when paired with data from the gage just below the dam (KOSH1) and will help with flood verification.

An alarm threshold of 24 feet was initially established based on events which caused inundation of properties in Otake Camp near the gage on December 2, 1999, May 6, 2002, and December 11, 2008. However, it was later determined that there was a rating curve change so the historical data are no longer valid as guidance for the current thresholds. The alarm threshold was raised to 28 ft following a peak flow event that reached that level and was near bankfull at Otake Camp.

Sheet0.Site: Kaukonahua Stream blw Wahiawa Reservoir, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes:
This gage samples Kaukonahua Stream just below Wahiawa Dam. 

Since this site has a short period of record, there is an insufficient number of cases to relate a stage/flow relationship with downstream impacts.

Sheet0.Site: Wahiawa Ditch at Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Wahiawa Reservoir at Spillway at Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes: The Wahiawa Reservoir, also known as Lake Wilson, is the largest fresh water body in the State of Hawaii. The reservoir retains waters from the North and South Forks of Kaukonahua Stream and is designed primarily to support agriculture along the north slope of Oahu. Since plantation agriculture disappeared in the 1990s, water levels in the reservoir are often times very high and close to the spillway level of 80 feet due to the lack of demand from farmers. High levels of water going over the spillway can cause flooding problems downstream in the Otake Camp area of Waialua. At a water level of 84 feet, the City & County of Honolulu Dept. of Emergency Management will evacuate residents of Otake Camp. This has happened 3 times between 1999 and 2005 during intense thunderstorms over the upper slopes of the Koolaus. A flash flood warning issued at the 84 feet level will provide about 30- to 45-minutes of lead time down at Otake Camp. A recent flood event indicated a water level rise as high as 0.65 feet in 15-minutes (2.60 feet per hour) so an alert level at 82 feet should be monitored closely since additional upstream rainfall will likely push the water level above the warning threshold of 84 feet. The Wahiawa Reservoir gage was installed by the USGS as part of a State Civil Defense flood warning project.
Sheet0.EOC Procedures:
At 82 feet, ask HPD to begin monitoring Otake Camp. NWS will also call DEM to provide notice the gauge is at this level. 

At 84 feet, evacuate Otake Camp and send WEA unless HPD has advised conditions warrant evacuation before this level. 

At 84 feet consult with NWS on whether a Flash Flood Watch should be issued due to potential dam failure. 

At 86 feet, coordinate with NWS on issuance of Flash Flood Warning with a considerable or catastrophic tag.

At 88 feet, water overtops dam. DEM activates IPAWS with dam failure message.

Sheet0.Site: Ku Tree Reservoir near Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes: Ku Tree Dam and Reservoir is an abandoned, unmaintained structure owned by the U.S. Army. The flow gates are left opened but heavy rains in the upper Koolaus can result in the reservoir filling up faster than water can flow out. Should the reservoir overflow, the dam is at risk of failure. Floodwaters will flow into Lake Wilson and possibly overwhelm the Wahiawa Dam creating an even greater flash flood. The U.S. Army would like to remove Ku Tree Dam but currently lacks the funds to do so and must conduct an environmental impact statement even if funds were available. The Army has not provided an alert threshold even though real-time monitoring is in place.

Sheet0.Site: SF Kaukonahua Str at E pump, nr Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Koolau Reservoir near Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
NF Kaukonahua Str abv RB, nr Wahiawa, Oahu, HI
Sheet0.NWS Notes: The North and South Forks of Kaukonahua Stream drain the central Koolau Range, one of the wettest areas on the island of Oahu. Both forks have USGS stream gages reporting in real time as part of a warning system for excessive amounts of water going over the Wahiawa Dam spillway, which can cause flooding in Otake Camp, Waialua. There are no known direct inundation risks along the North Fork, but the gage will provide early warning of excessive flow that may result in water going over the Wahiawa Dam spillway. Water levels in Lake Wilson can also rise relatively quickly, which may impact users of the state park at the lake. The North Fork gage was destroyed by the flash flood on December 11, 2008, but the USGS rebuilt the site.
